title: Get to Know Us
lede: - Meet the team members behind the science.

members.name: Thomas CHALK
bio: I'm Tom, an isotope geochemist and palaeoceanographer whose research explores the interactions between the ocean and climate over seasonal to geological timescales. I earned my PhD from the University of Southampton's National Oceanography Centre in 2015, following my undergraduate and master's studies at the University of Oxford.

I've held postdoctoral positions at several institutions, including the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution (WHOI) in the United States and the Arctic University of Tromsø (UiT) in Norway. Currently, I serve as a CNRS research scientist in the Climate team at CEREGE in Aix-en-Provence, France, and I'm a Visiting Fellow at the University of Southampton.

My work primarily focuses on reconstructing past atmospheric CO₂ levels and ocean pH by analyzing boron isotopes in marine carbonates, to improve our understanding of Earth's climate sensitivity and carbon cycle dynamics. I lead the ERC-funded ForCry project, which employs cryocell laser ablation techniques to analyze minute samples of carbonate minerals. When precipitated from seawater, and preserved in deep sea sediment, these can be used to generate high-resolution CO₂ records.
Besides doing research, I like to play board games, run up mountains, and veganise recipes.

links.label: ERC ForCry dedicated page on CEREGE website

members.name: Julie MEILLAND
bio: I'm a marine biologist whose research explores the life cycle and population dynamics of marine pelagic calcifiers such as planktonic Foraminifera and Pteropods. I graduated (PhD) from the University of Angers, France, in late 2015 and joined the Arctic University of Tromsø, Norway for my first postdoctoral research contract.

During my PhD and in Norway I specialised in the ecology and contribution of pelagic calcifiers, from polar regions and environments, to the marine carbon export. I later joined MARUM, at the University of Bremen, DE, before starting my CNRS research position in the Climate team at CEREGE in early 2025. There, and based on my findings on planktonic foraminifera reproduction in laboratory (Meilland et al., 2023 & 2024) I develop and manage the COntinuous REproduction for Foraminifera Facility (COREFF). I am also a modern foraminifera expert in taxonomy. With more than a year and half spent at sea through 20 research cruise from Antarctica to the Arctic, I have a tremendous field experience — strengthening my fundamental understanding of plankton ecology and population dynamics.
I love running and diving!

members.name: Olivier SULPIS
bio: I'm Olivier, a marine biogeochemist and ecologist, primarily interested in the carbon cycle of the ocean in the early Anthropocene. I use numerical models, laboratory experiments and in-situ observations to understand how sediments and organisms at the seafloor, a mostly unmapped environment that covers more than two thirds of our planet surface, regulate the climate of our planet. My research also explores deep-sea currents, waves and tides, marine snow, calcification and the response of calcifiers to global change. Leader of the Deep-C ERC project, I am developing novel experimental tools to reproduce abyssal and hadal environments in the laboratory, with a set of sensors operating under the highest pressures of the oceans.

I earned my PhD from McGill University, Montreal, in 2019, in aqueous chemistry. I pursued as a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Utrecht until 2023, when I started a CNRS research scientist position in the Climate team at CEREGE, south of France. In parallel with my research, I serve as an editor for Global Biogeochemical Cycles and Biogeosciences, and act as co-chair of a working group on the monitoring, reporting and verification of marine carbon dioxide removal, as part of the European Marine Board.
In my spare time, I enjoy playing bass, dancing, and cooking.

members.name: Matthieu BUISSON
members.affiliation: CNRS Postdoctoral Researcher at CEREGE, France
bio: I am a postdoctoral researcher in geochemistry and paleoceanography in the Climate team at CEREGE. My work focuses on the development and application of high-precision isotopic and elemental analyses to reconstruct past ocean chemistry and climate variability, with a particular emphasis on boron isotopes in marine carbonates.

Passionate about understanding past climate–ocean interactions, my aim is to improve reconstructions of seawater pH, atmospheric CO₂, and biogeochemical cycles over geological timescales, in order to anticipate ongoing and future climate change. My research lies at the interface between analytical (geo)chemistry and paleoceanography, combining methodological developments in mass spectrometry with their application to paleoenvironmental archives such as foraminifera.

members.name: Sonia CHAABANE
bio: I am a marine ecologist and micropalaeontologist at the French Research Institute for Development (IRD), based at CEREGE in Aix-en-Provence. My research focuses on how marine plankton responds to climate change, particularly warming, ocean acidification, and deoxygenation. I use planktonic foraminifera, microscopic calcifying organisms, as bioindicators to understand how marine ecosystems have changed in the past and how they may evolve in the future.

My work bridges global biodiversity databases, trait-based ecology, high-throughput imaging, and artificial intelligence. I have been deeply involved in the development and synthesis of large international databases (such as FORCIS and DYNAMITE), aiming to transform scattered observations into coherent knowledge that can inform both science and society. A key motivation of my research is to improve our capacity to detect, quantify, and anticipate biological responses to global change at large spatial and temporal scales.

Before joining IRD, I trained in marine and environmental sciences in Spain (ICTA) and held postdoctoral positions in France (CEREGE; FRB) and Germany (MPIC). Beyond research, I am strongly committed to open science, capacity building, and international collaboration, particularly in West Africa.
Outside the lab, I enjoy fieldwork at sea, and sharing science through collaborative projects and mentoring.

members.name: Maxime FELIX
members.affiliation: CNRS Marine Biogeochemistry Research Engineer at CEREGE, France
bio: I am a research engineer in the Climate team at CEREGE. My work focuses on management of hyperbaric equipment and measurement of carbonate chemistry at the Exocean laboratory. Passionate about ocean dynamics, my aim is to advance scientific research in deep sea waters, but also to enable the successful development of various projects within the laboratory.

Before joining CEREGE, I studied marine science with a specialization in anthropogenic disturbances at the University of Toulon, where I developed an interest in research as well as in laboratory instruments and analytical techniques.
Outside the lab, I enjoy sports such as tennis, running, and football, and I also appreciate discovering marine wildlife while freediving.

members.name: Marine JAUMON
members.affiliation: PhD Student at CEREGE and LOV, France
bio: I am a PhD student co-supervised by Olivier Sulpis (CEREGE) and Steeve Comeau (LOV). My work focuses on how biogenic calcium carbonate forms and dissolves under environmental changes, with a particular emphasis on coral and reef ecosystems.

I completed a BSc in Environmental and Physical Geography at the University of Montreal and after graduating, I joined the Aquarium of Guadeloupe for a civic service program, where I was raising awareness about marine biodiversity among children and adults, and worked on coral restoration projects involving Favia fragum. I then pursued a Master's degree in Marine Sciences, focusing on Marine Biology and Ecology at the University of Bordeaux, where I developed an interest in biogeochemistry. This led me to an M2 internship with Olivier, studying the effect of microbial respiration on carbonate dissolution, along with fieldwork in Bermuda at BIOS.
When I'm not in the lab, you'll probably find me in the ocean looking for sea creatures, diving, or attempting to surf. I also love hiking and reading with a good cup of coffee.

members.name: Jaime Y. SUÁREZ-IBARRA
members.affiliation: CNRS Postdoctoral Researcher at CEREGE, France
bio: I am a micropaleontologist and paleoceanographer specializing in late Neogene planktonic foraminifera. I work as a CNRS postdoctoral researcher in the Climate team at CEREGE, south of France. My research focuses on past climate changes and planktonic foraminifera ecological and morphological evolution.
I am curious about the processes that shaped the Earth climate system, languages, cultures and traveling.

members.name: Astrid HYLÉN
bio: I am an MSCA postdoctoral researcher in the Climate team at CEREGE. I am passionate about how humans affect the ocean's capacity to store carbon. I use experiments, fieldwork and modelling to understand when carbon is degraded or preserved in the seafloor. My aim is to advance our understanding of carbon cycling in coastal environments, to support the management and restoration of coastal systems.

Before joining CEREGE, I did my PhD at the University of Gothenburg, Sweden, and a postdoc at the University of Antwerp, Belgium. My speciality is measuring sediment-water fluxes of dissolved compounds, and I have previously worked on sedimentary nutrient cycling and ocean alkalinity enhancement for CO₂ removal.
In my spare time, I enjoy reading and travelling, as well as cooking, baking, and eating – anything food-related.

members.name: Katoo DECLERCK
bio: I am a biologist pursuing an internship at the exocean laboratory in CEREGE. My work focuses on the dissolution of foraminifera and the role of organic matter during this process. Passionate about the ocean, my aim is to get a better understanding of the importance of marine environments in mitigating climate change by dissolving calcium carbonates.
Before joining CEREGE I studied global change biology at the University of Antwerp, where I learned about different consequences of climate change and to help mitigate these effects.
Outside the lab you can find me somewhere hiking, chasing beautiful sunsets or enjoying a big cup of tea, usually accompanied with a homemade song and some jokes!

members.name: Vincent LE FOUEST
members.affiliation: Professor at La Rochelle Université, France
bio: I am Associate Professor at La Rochelle University and part of the LIENSs laboratory since 2013. My expertise relies on ocean-biogeochemical modeling of the coastal ocean, including the land-to-sea interface. I focus on temperate to arctic environments, where I try to understand how changes in land-to-sea fluxes modulate coastal biogeochemistry, plankton and air-sea gas fluxes. To do so, I combine complex numerical ocean-sea ice-biogeochemical models with in situ and space remote sensing observations.

members.name: Mariette WOLTHERS
members.affiliation: Professor at Utrecht University, the Netherlands
bio: My main research focus is on the interaction between water and minerals (crystals, Earth Materials). I investigate the influence of mineral formation/dissolution on water quality and vice versa. I explore mineral nucleation, growth, dissolution and surface reactivity, with and without impurity ions and at different ratios of the crystal-building ions. My approach is both experimental and theoretical; the tools I use to study earth materials range from atomic scale computational chemistry and macroscale geochemical modelling to sophisticated analyses techniques such as electron microscopy, light scattering and synchrotron-based spectroscopy.
